449	### Criterion 5: Validate
450	
451	Scores the **signed-off analysis** — the complete output with all conclusions traced and weak
452	links resolved or explicitly flagged with confidence caveats — across all six output sections,
453	focusing on the confidence caveats attached to the Derivation Chains (output section 4).
454	
455	- **Rigorous** — every derivation chain's weakest link is named; every MEDIUM or LOW confidence
456	  caveat, on a chain or on the Conclusion section, explains only its own rating: it names each
457	  GT-N? input it rests on directly, with the verification that would remove that input as a
458	  cause of the downgrade, and each Cn its head cites — or, for the Conclusion section, each
459	  contributing chain — that is rated below HIGH, and it need not re-explain a named Cn, whose
460	  own caveat carries its explanation; and for each downgrade cause belonging to the chain or
461	  Conclusion itself, such as a weak inference step or an absent-fails derivation, it states
462	  what would remove it as a cause of the downgrade or a stated reason no verification path
463	  exists, that reason being either, for an absent-fails derivation, the absent-fails EXCEPT
464	  clause below, the only clause that can stand in for a verification path, or an explicit
465	  account of why no available evidence settles that cause;
466	  the overall Conclusion section's confidence rating (HIGH / MEDIUM / LOW) matches the weakest
467	  chain that contributes to it, counting only chains not covered by an EXCEPT clause stated in
468	  this same descriptor; no chain that consumes a GT-N? input is rated HIGH confidence; every
469	  chain is rated no higher than the lowest-rated chain its head cites, a ceiling that holds
470	  even when a cited chain is rated MEDIUM under an EXCEPT clause below.
471	  Every rating is calibrated: each chain carries the band its inputs, hops and rivals
472	  license under the three-axis definition in `output-template.md` — no chain rated above
473	  what those axes permit, and none rated below it. A Conclusion claim supported by
474	  at least one HIGH-confidence chain may be presented at HIGH; a claim with no such
475	  chain is presented at the band its weakest contributing chain licenses, and presenting
476	  it so is Rigorous rather than a shortfall. Under-rating is a defect of the same kind
477	  as over-rating, and this criterion scores calibration, not altitude. EXCEPT: a chain is explicitly marked speculative — for
478	  example `[Speculative]` — and the analysis states, in the same place, that the claim it
479	  supports is not load-bearing and is offered for exploration only; that mark plus that
480	  statement is the satisfying evidence, and the chain may remain MEDIUM, though its confidence
481	  line still gives each of its own downgrade causes what would remove it or an explicit account
482	  of why no available evidence settles it, because the mark is not a no-path reason; a
483	  speculative chain cited on another chain's head is load-bearing and no longer satisfies this
484	  EXCEPT clause, so a speculative chain with no verification path is not cited on another
485	  chain's head and instead stays speculative or moves to Abandoned Reasoning (output section 5).
486	  EXCEPT: a chain is
487	  an absent-fails derivation — of the form "if [assumption] were true we could conclude X;
488	  [assumption] is false; therefore X does not follow" — whose named false assumption is the
489	  satisfying evidence, and the chain may remain MEDIUM because it establishes what does not
490	  follow rather than what does.
491	
492	  The adversarial pass Phase 5 prescribes has run and its record is complete: each computed
493	  figure's recompute, the sensitivity ground truth and whether it is `?`-marked, the rival and
494	  where it is ruled out or carried live, a premise stated in the past tense, an unfiltered
495	  cause list written before any grouping, clusters each naming the chain ids or ground-truth
496	  ids the weakness bears on, per cluster a named plan change or an explicitly accepted risk
497	  with a named mitigation, and the falsification condition — each part present or carrying its
498	  step's not-applicable line. Each structural weakness the pass
499	  returned has landed somewhere a reader can find it — as a named weak link on a chain, or as
500	  an explicit confidence caveat on the conclusion it threatens. An analysis whose conclusion is
501	  neither a plan nor a claim satisfies the Premise, Causes, Clusters and Disposition parts by
502	  carrying the `adversarial pass not applicable — [reason]` line with its reason named — that
503	  line is the adversarial-technique step's own not-applicable line, not a waiver of the whole
504	  record, so the Recompute, Sensitivity, Rival and Falsification parts each still carry their
505	  content or their own step's not-applicable line; an analysis that does carry a plan or a claim
506	  cannot satisfy the technique step that way, and the reason given is what makes the two cases
507	  distinguishable.
508	
509	  **A conclusion without a HIGH chain is not a shortfall.** A conclusion resting on no
510	  HIGH-confidence chain, uncovered by either EXCEPT clause above, is Rigorous on this
511	  criterion when every band it rests on is the band that chain's axes license and the
512	  Conclusion's own rating equals its weakest contributing chain's. A MEDIUM or LOW overall
513	  Conclusion rating remains a legitimate, honestly-caveated analysis — `output-template.md`
514	  permits it and this criterion now scores it Rigorous when it is calibrated. What bands
515	  this criterion below Rigorous is a band that does not match its axes in either direction,
516	  never a band that is merely low, and a verdict block reporting Rigorous alongside a
517	  MEDIUM overall rating is the expected shape of an honest analysis rather than a
518	  contradiction. An exception is claimed, not assumed: an analysis relying on one of the
519	  two EXCEPT clauses above names it in the Criterion 5 verdict block and cites the evidence
520	  that clause requires; an unclaimed exception is not applied on the analysis's behalf.
521	
522	- **Sound** — confidence ratings exist on chains, but a MEDIUM or LOW confidence line omits a
523	  GT-N? input it rests on directly, or a Cn its head cites (or, on the Conclusion section, a
524	  contributing chain) that is rated below HIGH, or a downgrade cause belonging to its own chain
525	  or Conclusion — including a MEDIUM or LOW rating that no named GT-N? input or Cn accounts for
526	  and whose line names no cause of its own; OR a confidence line names a GT-N? input without the
527	  verification that would remove it as a cause of the downgrade; OR a confidence line gives a
528	  downgrade cause belonging to its own chain or Conclusion with neither what would remove it as
529	  a cause of the downgrade nor a permitted no-path reason — for an absent-fails derivation, the
530	  absent-fails EXCEPT clause, or an explicit account of why no available evidence settles that
531	  cause — including a line whose only account of such a cause is the speculative EXCEPT clause
532	  or any clause other than the absent-fails one; OR a chain's head cites a chain marked
533	  speculative that has no verification path; OR a chain is rated HIGH confidence while consuming
534	  a GT-N? input (the rating does not match the unverified-input rule); OR a chain is rated above
535	  the lowest-rated chain its head cites; OR a single chain's band does not match what its
536	  three axes license, in either direction — a chain rated HIGH whose head carries a `?` or
537	  whose hops rest on a stated `[Assumes: A-N]` premise, or a chain meeting all three axes
538	  rated MEDIUM — while every other chain in the analysis is correctly banded; OR an
539	  adversarial pass record, or the `adversarial pass not applicable — [reason]` line, is present
540	  but one or more of the Recompute, Sensitivity, Rival and Falsification parts is absent and
541	  carries no not-applicable line of its own — a step silently omitted from a pass that otherwise
542	  ran.
543	
544	- **Hand-wavy** — confidence ratings appear on the overall Conclusion section but are absent
545	  from individual derivation chains; OR weak links are described in general terms ("some
546	  assumptions remain uncertain") without naming the specific chain step or GT-N? input that
547	  caused the concern; OR an adversarial pass record is present but no cluster carries a
548	  disposition — neither a named plan change nor an explicitly accepted risk with a named
549	  mitigation — so the pass named structural weaknesses and acted on none of them; OR the record
550	  states its clusters without the cause list they were drawn from, which is the generic risk
551	  list the pass exists to replace rather than a pass that produced one; OR two or more
552	  chains carry bands their axes do not license, so the miscalibration is a pattern rather
553	  than an isolated entry; OR every chain in the analysis carries the same band and no
554	  confidence line names which axis produced it, which is a default setting rather than a
555	  rating.
556	
557	- **Absent** — no confidence ratings appear anywhere in the derivation chains; OR GT-N? inputs
558	  are used in load-bearing chains without any confidence caveat anywhere in the document; OR
559	  — covering the case the first two clauses miss — confidence ratings exist but no weak-link
560	  identification or chain inspection was performed at all, so there is no evidence that
561	  Phase 5's stress-test operation was executed; OR neither an adversarial pass record nor an
562	  `adversarial pass not applicable — [reason]` line appears anywhere in the response, so there
563	  is no evidence that Phase 5's adversarial pass was executed at all. These two clauses are
564	  separate readings: a weakest-link paragraph written by the same reasoning that built the
565	  chains satisfies the first and not the second, and an analysis scoring above Absent on the
566	  strength of that paragraph alone is what this clause exists to catch.
567	
568	### Criterion 6: Conclusion-to-Ground-Truth Traceability
569	
570	Scores the relationship between the **Conclusion section** (section 6) claims and the
571	**Derivation Chains** (section 4) that produced them — a cross-section structural property
572	of the signed-off analysis as a whole. Quoted span: where the band is determined by whether a section-6 claim traces to a named section-4 chain, it must be drawn from the self-audit scan's claim-inventory table row or rows that determine the band, not from the Conclusion prose directly. Where the band is determined by the Key Insight being a restatement of the recommended approach rather than a non-obvious finding — a semantic property the claim-inventory table carries no column for — quote the analysis text directly.
573	
574	- **Rigorous** — every claim in the Conclusion section (recommended approach, key insight,
575	  trade-offs acknowledged) traces to a specific named derivation chain in section 4; the
576	  Conclusion section introduces no new claims that did not appear in section 4; the Key
577	  Insight names a non-obvious finding — a result that reasoning by analogy or convention
578	  does not reach — rather than restating the recommended approach.
579	
580	- **Sound** — most Conclusion claims trace to chains in section 4, but one claim is introduced
581	  for the first time in the Conclusion section (new reasoning not present in any derivation
582	  chain); OR the Key Insight is a restatement of the recommended approach rather than a
583	  non-obvious finding.
584	
585	- **Hand-wavy** — the Conclusion section contains claims that contradict or are inconsistent
586	  with the derivation chains in section 4; OR multiple new claims appear in the Conclusion
587	  section that are not present in any derivation chain.
588	
589	- **Absent** — the Conclusion section contains claims with no corresponding derivation chain
590	  anywhere in section 4; OR the Conclusion section is absent or empty; OR every item in the
591	  Conclusion is new reasoning not established by any derivation chain — the Conclusion section
592	  has been used to introduce the analysis's conclusions rather than to synthesize them.
593	
594	The extraction and caveat rules the bands above are scored against are stated here verbatim so the grading instrument carries them, not just the surface it grades.
595	
596	A Conclusion-section claim is a bold lead-in whose colon closes the bold span, or a numbered or bulleted list item, and the four lead-ins this template prescribes — `**Recommended approach:**`, `**Key insight:**`, `**Trade-offs acknowledged:**` and `**Confidence:**` — are always claims and each must cite a chain; the `**Confidence:**` line discharges that obligation through the chains D-07 already requires it to name, and a HIGH line whose justification prose names no chain is the one position where this rule and the extractor can disagree, so name the chain there too; nothing inside a fenced block is ever a claim whatever its shape, a near-paraphrase restatement or direct entailment of an already-cited claim earlier in the same section is not a second claim, and prose carrying neither a bold colon lead-in nor a list marker is not a claim at all. Three bounds are measured, not assumed: a bold lead-in whose colon-terminated span is the entire physical line and carries no citation of its own is a section-intro label, and the citation obligation then falls to the list items beneath it; a bold span whose closing `**` is not immediately preceded by the colon is not matched at all — write `**Label:** text` to match, not `**Label: text**`; and a list item counts only when it closes its own sentence or runs past forty characters. Enumerate by this rule, not by recollection — the rule is the contract and the extractor is a partial instrument for it.
597	
598	A caveat qualifying an existing Conclusion-section claim either names the chain it qualifies inline or carries the marker `no chain — flagged assumption only` (em dash, lower case, no trailing punctuation inside the marker), and a marked caveat still scores untraced: the marker discloses the gap, it does not discharge the claim, because it is honest labelling rather than a citation and the extractor is deliberately not taught to recognise it. A caveat doing neither is cut, not softened.
599	
600	---
601	
602	## Usage Note
603	
604	Score every criterion. Produce one verdict block per criterion, using the prescribed format
605	from the Verdict Block Format section above. The analysis must clear the gate (no criterion
606	at Absent) and the hand-wavy cap (at most one criterion at Hand-wavy) before conclusions are
607	presented. If either condition is not met, revise the relevant sections and re-score — bounded
608	to **at most one re-perception pass** per analysis, per the rule stated in full under "How to
609	Apply This Gate" at the top of this document. If a criterion still fails after that single
610	pass, present it as an unresolved gap with a stated confidence caveat instead of re-scoring

3	# Inversion
4	
5	> A negative-direction stress test on a *claim*. Following Jacobi's maxim
6	> "Invert, always invert" — popularised in decision-making practice by Charlie
7	> Munger and Farnam Street — inversion asks not "what makes this claim true?"
8	> but "what would have to be true for this claim to fail?" The preconditions
9	> it surfaces enter the spine at Phase 2 as `untested belief` rows.
10	
11	---
12	
13	- [When to reach for this](#when-to-reach-for-this)
14	- [Procedure](#procedure)
15	- [Worked mini-example](#worked-mini-example)
16	- [Failure modes](#failure-modes)
17	- [Output contract](#output-contract)
18	- [Handoff](#handoff)
19	
20	---
21	
22	## When to reach for this
23	
24	Use inversion during Phase 2 (Challenge Assumptions) when a claim is sitting in
25	the Classified Assumptions Table and you want to surface the hidden preconditions
26	it depends on — by reasoning backward from its failure rather than forward from
27	its support. Also a useful sanity check after Phase 4: invert the headline
28	conclusion and ask whether any necessary precondition is unverified.
29	
30	**Decision rule — inversion vs. pre-mortem:** inversion stress-tests a **claim**;
31	[pre-mortem](${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/agents/references/pre-mortem.md) stress-tests a **plan**. With only a stated belief,
32	conclusion, or design principle in hand, inversion is the right tool. If a
33	concrete plan with actions and a timeline exists, pre-mortem fits better — it
34	reasons about implementation failure modes that claim-level inversion cannot see.
35	
36	**Not a good fit:** stress-testing a plan with timelines and dependencies — use
37	[pre-mortem](${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/agents/references/pre-mortem.md). Tracing what already went wrong on a single causal
38	chain — use 5-Whys. Inversion is the negative-direction pass on a claim;
39	[second-order](${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/agents/references/second-order.md) thinking is the positive-direction pass
40	on the same conclusion — run inversion first to find what could fail, then
41	second-order to trace consequences of what holds.
42	
43	---
44	
45	## Procedure
46	
47	1. **State the claim precisely.** Write the claim in one sentence in the form
48	   "X is true" or "X will hold." Avoid hedges. The sharper the claim, the
49	   sharper the inverted form.
50	
51	2. **Invert it.** Rewrite the claim as its failure: "X is false" or "X does not
52	   hold." Resist softening the inverted form — "X might not hold" is not an
53	   inversion, it is a hedge.
54	
55	3. **Enumerate failure-guaranteeing conditions.** List every condition that
56	   would *guarantee* the inverted form. These are not risks; they are
57	   sufficient causes of failure. Write at least five before stopping.
58	
59	4. **Derive the necessary preconditions, and state each as a claim that can be
60	   false.** For each failure-guaranteeing condition, name the precondition whose
61	   absence would cause it, and write it as a definite assertion about the world
62	   ("runbooks transfer without rewriting"), never as a topic ("runbooks"). A
63	   topic cannot be checked; an assertion can. One condition may yield more than
64	   one precondition, and two conditions may share one — record the mapping
65	   rather than assuming it is one-to-one, because a precondition that several
66	   failure conditions depend on is the one most worth verifying first. This
67	   converts a failure list into a list of things the original claim silently
68	   depends on.
69	
70	5. **Tag each precondition `load-bearing` or not.** A precondition is
71	   **load-bearing** when the conclusion does not survive its being false — the
72	   same sense the validation rubric defines for chains. One that would merely
73	   weaken the conclusion, or affect only an intermediate result nothing rests
74	   on, is not load-bearing. Mark each one explicitly; an untagged precondition
75	   reads as equally important as every other, which is how a list of twelve
76	   preconditions hides the two that actually matter.
77	
78	6. **Check each precondition's status.** For every necessary precondition, ask:
79	   is it verified, conventionally assumed, or untested? Anything not currently
80	   verified is unverified by default. **A precondition that is both
81	   `load-bearing` and unverified is the analysis's sharpest finding** — report
82	   those first, ahead of the full list.
83	
84	7. **Record each unverified precondition as an `untested belief`.** Each
85	   unverified precondition becomes one row in the Classified Assumptions Table
86	   with type `untested belief`, carrying its `load-bearing` tag, routed back to
87	   Phase 2 for the challenge-and-verify operation.
88	
89	---
90	
91	## Worked mini-example
92	
93	**Claim:** "Switching our primary database from Postgres to a managed NoSQL
94	service will reduce operational toil."
95	
96	- **Inverted form:** "Switching to managed NoSQL will *not* reduce operational
97	  toil — toil will stay the same or increase."
98	- **Failure-guaranteeing conditions:**
99	  - The new service requires more frequent capacity tuning than the current setup
100	  - Application code requires substantial rewrites that introduce new bugs
101	  - Existing monitoring and runbooks do not transfer and must be rebuilt
102	  - The managed service's failure modes are unfamiliar to the on-call rotation
103	- **Necessary preconditions of the original claim:** tuning load is lower; query
104	  patterns port cleanly; observability and runbooks transfer; on-call engineers
105	  reach operational fluency within the migration window.
106	- **Returned `untested belief` rows (to Phase 2):**
107	  - `untested belief`: new service's tuning frequency is lower than current Postgres
108	  - `untested belief`: current query patterns port cleanly to the target data model
109	  - `untested belief`: observability tooling has equivalent coverage post-migration
110	  - `untested belief`: on-call rotation can reach operational fluency in window
111	
112	---
113	
114	## Failure modes
115	
116	**Inverting only the surface claim instead of its necessary preconditions.**
117	Flipping "X is good" to "X is bad" and stopping there produces no new information
118	— the value of inversion is in the *preconditions* the failure form forces into
119	view. Always carry the inversion through to step 4 of the procedure.
120	
121	**Leaving every precondition untagged.** A flat list of twelve preconditions
122	reads as twelve equal risks, which hides the two the conclusion actually rests
123	on. Tag each one `load-bearing` or not at step 5, and report the load-bearing
124	unverified ones first.
125	
126	**Writing a precondition as a topic instead of a claim.** "Runbooks" cannot be
127	true or false, so it cannot be checked, and it will survive every later review
128	by being unfalsifiable. "Runbooks transfer without rewriting" can be checked.
129	
130	**Treating the inverted claim as the new conclusion rather than a stress test.**
131	Inversion is diagnostic, not assertive. The inverted form is a thinking device
132	for surfacing dependencies, not a finding. "The claim is false because I could
133	invert it" is the same error as "the cause is real because I drew it on a fishbone."
134	
135	**Confusing inversion with pre-mortem when a plan exists.** If the artifact under
136	analysis is a plan with timelines and dependencies, claim-level inversion will
137	miss the implementation-failure modes that [pre-mortem](${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/agents/references/pre-mortem.md) is
138	designed to surface. Use the claim-vs-plan decision rule above.
139	
140	---
141	
142	## Output contract
143	
144	The focused inversion output MUST include these four level-2 section headers, verbatim,
145	as real `##` headings in the response. Strict on the header strings; soft on content.
146	This structure enables reliable downstream detection.
147	
148	Required headers:
149	
150	- `## Inverted Claim`
151	- `## Failure-Guaranteeing Conditions`
152	- `## Necessary Preconditions`
153	- `## Stress-Test Verdict`
154	
155	---
156	
157	## Handoff
158	
159	The unverified preconditions surfaced here enter the 5-phase methodology at
160	Phase 2 (Challenge Assumptions). Each precondition is recorded as an
161	`untested belief` — the fourth assumption class in Phase 2's four-type scheme —
162	because inversion surfaces silent dependencies, not verified facts. Add each
163	unverified precondition as a row in the Classified Assumptions Table with type
164	`untested belief`.
165	
166	Do not route inverted preconditions directly to Phase 3 (Establish Ground Truths).
167	Promotion happens inside Phase 2's challenge-and-verify operation, not by
168	skipping it. A precondition is promoted only after evidence confirms it — until
169	then it stays `untested belief`, and any chain depending on it inherits the D-07 caveat.
170	
171	For the positive-direction counterpart, pair inversion with
172	[second-order-thinking](${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/agents/references/second-order.md): inversion surfaces what must
173	hold; second-order traces downstream consequences once it does. Inversion
174	stress-tests claims; [pre-mortem](${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/agents/references/pre-mortem.md) stress-tests plans.

Based on the web search results, here are the key findings regarding reaction yield reproducibility with confidence intervals:

## Reproducibility Threshold

A calculated yield within roughly ±10 percentage points of the literature value is generally considered reproducible.

## Confidence Intervals for Reaction Yield

The confidence interval quantifies uncertainty due to random error by providing a probabilistic range for the true mean. However, it's important to note that it does not account for any systematic error that introduces consistent bias to the mean yield.

## Statistical Approach

The standard normal interval is an appropriate measure of the limits of reproducibility for reaction yield data but can produce interval boundaries outside the restricted range of the reaction yield, especially in the case of few repeat experiments. In this event, it is recommended to constrain boundaries within 0–100%, as common best practice for reporting the confidence interval.

## Variability Sources

Common deviation sources include differences in reagent purity, ambient humidity affecting hygroscopic intermediates, variations in stirring efficiency at different scales, and operator-dependent loss during workup.

The search results emphasize that reporting confidence intervals for reaction yields is becoming a standard practice in chemistry for documenting reproducibility across replicate runs.

# First-Principles Analysis: The 62%→71% Catalyst Yield Claim

*(MODE = full-composer; no single-technique trigger fired in the request, so all five phases run, with inversion, estimate, and second-order thinking applied where each phase invokes them.)*

## 1. Problem Essence

**Core problem:** Does the reported comparison (mean yield 62% → 71%, three runs) by itself provide sufficient evidence that a specific manipulated variable — the new catalyst — caused a real, statistically distinguishable, reproducible, generalizable improvement in this reaction's yield, and, if not, exactly which weaker claims does the data still support versus merely permit as speculation?

**Success criteria** (checkable against the Conclusion, section 6):
1. Section 6 lists, as specific claims, what is supported by the report's literal content alone — each such claim cites only the literal-content chains (C1, C6) and introduces no unstated assumption.
2. Section 6 lists, as specific claims, which stronger claims (statistical significance, real-effect-vs-noise, causal attribution to the catalyst, generalizability/economic value, reliability as a planning figure) are *not* supported, and each names the concrete missing datum (SD/raw values, controls statement, substrate scope, replicate count) that would resolve it.
3. At least one quantitative treatment (the estimate technique) shows, with an actual worked and independently-recomputed confidence-interval calculation, how wide the uncertainty band around an n=3 mean can be — this is a checkable property of the Ground Truths/Derivation Chains, not an assertion.
4. No chain in section 4 that section 6 relies on asserts, at HIGH confidence, either "the catalyst works" or "the catalyst doesn't work" — the Conclusion's confidence rating is calibrated to what the evidence actually licenses, not to a verdict either direction.

---

## 2. Assumptions Table

Phase 2 inversion was applied to the headline claim ("the catalyst raises yield from 62% to 71%"). Inverted form: "the catalyst does not raise yield; the 9-point gap is not attributable to it." Failure-guaranteeing conditions enumerated: (a) run-to-run process variability alone could produce a 9-point gap; (b) the baseline and catalyzed runs were not run under matched conditions; (c) the three reported runs were selected from a larger, partially unreported set; (d) yield was measured by different methods in the two conditions; (e) the runs are not independent (shared reagent lot, shared workup); (f) a 9-point gap is not chemically distinguishable from ordinary measurement noise for this class of reaction. Each necessary precondition of the original claim is recorded below as an `untested belief`, tagged load-bearing where the conclusion does not survive its failure.

| # | Assumption | Type | Treatment | Verdict | Verification |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A1 | The 62% baseline was obtained under the same conditions (temperature, stoichiometry, solvent, workup, timing, substrate batch) as the 71% catalyzed runs — a true controlled comparison. **[load-bearing]** | untested belief | Verify or flag | Challenge — the report gives no statement either way; this is inversion's single most load-bearing precondition | unverified — flagged |
| A2 | "Three runs" means three independent replicates of the catalyzed condition (and, separately, of the baseline) — not one batch measured three times, not a mixed count. | untested belief | Verify or flag | Challenge — the phrase is genuinely ambiguous as worded | unverified — flagged |
| A3 | 62% and 71% are arithmetic means of the three runs, not a best-of-three or a single rounded representative run. | untested belief | Verify or flag | Challenge — no statement of how the reported figure was derived from the three runs | unverified — flagged |
| A4 | Yield was measured by the same method (e.g., isolated yield after identical purification) in both conditions. **[load-bearing]** | untested belief | Verify or flag | Challenge — measurement-method mismatch is a known source of spurious "improvement" | unverified — flagged |
| A5 | The three reported runs are the complete set of attempts made — no lower-yielding or failed runs were excluded before reporting. **[load-bearing]** | untested belief | Verify or flag | Challenge — selective reporting is a well-documented risk pattern and cannot be excluded from the report alone | unverified — flagged |
| A6 | The runs are statistically independent (not correlated through a shared reagent batch, shared workup step, or same-day operator effects). **[load-bearing]** | untested belief | Verify or flag | Challenge — nothing in the report addresses this | unverified — flagged |
| A7 | Reporting a mean yield across three runs with no stated spread is an acceptable convention in this context. | convention | Challenge before accepting | Challenge — GT-3 shows current best-practice guidance explicitly argues this convention should be replaced by mean+95% CI reporting precisely because it hides this information | unverified — flagged |
| A8 | The underlying raw per-run data / supporting information (SI) is unavailable to this analysis. | current constraint | Record expiry | Accept — expires once the lab's SI, notebook, or raw data are obtained | current, as of this analysis |
| A9 | Yield alone is sufficient to judge whether "the catalyst" is valuable, without selectivity, loading/cost, turnover number, or recyclability data. | untested belief / convention | Challenge | Challenge — catalyst value is multidimensional; the report addresses only one dimension | unverified — flagged |
| A10 | The 9-point improvement generalizes beyond this one substrate/reaction/scale. | untested belief | Verify or flag | Challenge — no substrate-scope or scale-up data given | unverified — flagged |
| A11 | A 9-point (≈14.5% relative) yield difference is chemically meaningful rather than within ordinary run-to-run noise for this class of reaction. **[load-bearing]** | untested belief | Verify or flag | Challenge — this is exactly what cannot be judged without variance data (see GT-3, chains C2/C3) | unverified — flagged |
| A12 | Typical run-to-run standard deviation for manually executed bench-scale organic-yield measurements is on the order of several to ~10+ percentage points. | untested belief | Verify or flag | Challenge — attempted verification; the directly on-point source was unreachable and the open alternative uses synthetic, not measured, data (Phase 3 failure record below) | unverified — flagged, not promoted to a ground truth |
| A13 | The illustrative n=3/n=7 dataset used in chain C3 (synthetic "imagined" data from a methods primer) is a reasonable stand-in for the kind of scatter a real reaction's yield replicates could plausibly show. *(surfaced by End-of-phase Assumption Audit, chain C3 step 3)* | untested belief | Verify or flag | Challenge — the source itself labels this data "imagined"; used only as a mathematical illustration, not an empirical claim | unverified — flagged |
| A14 | At least some downstream readers/decision-makers would act on the 71% figure (scale-up planning, further citation) without first seeking replication or variance data. *(surfaced by Assumption Audit, chain C5 step 1)* | untested belief | Verify or flag | Challenge — plausible but not confirmed for this specific report | unverified — flagged |
| A15 | The reported 71% is a first/early small-sample result not already cross-checked against a larger confirmatory dataset — i.e., the kind of result regression-to-the-mean applies to. *(surfaced by Assumption Audit, chain C5 step 2)* | untested belief | Verify or flag | Challenge — consistent with "three runs" being described as if it were the whole evidentiary basis, but not confirmed | unverified — flagged |

---

## 3. Ground Truths

**GT-1** The report states that yield rose from 62% to 71%, "measured across three runs." — source: the problem statement supplied for this analysis; read-at-source: direct quotation, the claim text itself.

**GT-2** The report specifies no standard deviation, range, or confidence interval for either figure; does not state whether "three runs" refers to the catalyzed condition only, to both conditions, or to something else; and does not state whether reaction conditions (temperature, stoichiometry, catalyst loading, solvent, workup, timing, substrate batch) or the yield-measurement method were held constant between the two conditions. — source: same problem statement; read-at-source: verified by direct inspection — nothing beyond the quoted sentence is given.

**GT-3** For a small sample (n<30), the (1−α)100% confidence interval for a sample mean requires the sample standard deviation s_x (or the raw data points from which it is computed), in addition to n: x̄ ± t_(α/2)(s_x/√n), with (n−1) degrees of freedom; no CI or significance test can be computed without s_x or the raw values. — source: Sally Bloodworth, "Reporting uncertainty: an updated convention for organic chemists," Zenodo record 14999714 ("Primer.pdf"); read-at-source: p.7, Appendix "Confidence interval" formula, quoted directly.

**GT-4** In that primer's worked exemplar, three replicate yields for "Compound 3" (56%, 66%, 45%) give a mean of 56% and a stated 95% CI of 30%–82% — a 52-percentage-point-wide interval; the primer explicitly labels this "an imagined dataset" (synthetic/illustrative, not measured lab data). — source: same Zenodo Primer; read-at-source: p.2, Figure 1 (data table) and Figure 2 (Compound 3 panel); independently recomputed here (t₀.₀₂₅,₂ = 4.303, s_x ≈ 10.5, SE ≈ 6.07, 56 ± 26.1 ≈ 30–82) and matches the source exactly.

**GT-5** In the same exemplar, "Compound 1" with seven replicate yields (56, 66, 45, 58, 59, 60, 58) gives a mean of 57% and a stated 95% CI of 52%–63% — an 11-point-wide interval, markedly narrower than Compound 3's despite comparable individual-value scatter (45–66). — source: same Zenodo Primer; read-at-source: p.2, Figure 1/Figure 2, Compound 1; independently recomputed here (mean 57.4, s_x ≈ 6.32, SE ≈ 2.39, t₀.₀₂₅,₆=2.447, CI ≈ 51.6–63.3) and matches the source.

**GT-6** Attributing an observed difference in an outcome specifically to one manipulated variable (here, the catalyst) requires that other variables capable of affecting the outcome were held constant between the compared conditions; if other variables could also have differed, the observed difference is logically consistent with any of those variables, singly or in combination, and cannot be uniquely assigned to the variable of interest without further evidence. — source: derivation shown inline (definition of a controlled comparison; yield is known to depend on multiple factors — temperature, stoichiometry, workup, measurement method — so an uncontrolled comparison under-determines the cause); classified as a matter of formal/methodological logic, not an external citation.

**GT-7** Regression toward the mean: when a value is observed to be unusually extreme partly because of random (noise) variation, an independent later measurement of the same underlying quantity will, on average, be less extreme than the originally observed value, because the specific noise draw that produced the extremity is not expected to recur. — source: derivation shown inline via variance decomposition (observed = true effect + independent noise; conditioning on an unusually high observed value raises the expected noise contribution, which does not repeat identically on remeasurement); the phenomenon is the standard one first described by Galton (1886) — no external citation opened for that historical attribution.

**Phase 3 failure record:** The source `https://www.thieme-connect.com/products/ejournals/pdf/10.1055/a-2907-9424.pdf` ("Letter: Standard Reporting of the Uncertainty in Reaction Yield," Thieme) — sought to verify A12 (typical real-world run-to-run yield variance) — could not be opened; WebFetch returned a bot-protection/"enable JavaScript and cookies" interstitial rather than article content. Reason: unreachable. The open alternative located (the Zenodo primer above, by the same author/topic) was read in full and satisfies GT-3/GT-4/GT-5, but it uses explicitly synthetic ("imagined") illustrative data, so it does **not** verify A12's empirical magnitude claim; A12 remains unverified and was deliberately not promoted to a ground truth (see Abandoned Reasoning, Dead End 1).

**Provenance summary:** `?`-marked: none (0 of 7). Read-at-source: GT-1 (problem statement, direct quote), GT-2 (problem statement, absence verified by inspection), GT-3 (Primer p.7), GT-4 (Primer p.2), GT-5 (Primer p.2). GT-6 and GT-7 are verified by inline derivation rather than external citation; neither feeds a HIGH-confidence chain on its own (GT-6 → C4, MEDIUM; GT-7 → C5, LOW), so Criterion 3's read-at-source-location requirement for HIGH chains does not apply to them.

---

## 4. Derivation Chains

### Conclusion C1: The report's literal content is limited to a bare point-to-point comparison

GT-1 (report's stated numbers: 62%→71%, three runs) + GT-2 (report omits SD, controls, run-definition)
→ the only information content the report carries is a comparison of two point-value averages, obtained under conditions the report does not specify
→ taken at face value, the report licenses stating only that a mean-yield increase was observed and reported — nothing beyond that

**Pre-check:** head GT-1, GT-2 · ?-marked: none · lowest cited: none · Inputs ceiling: HIGH
**Confidence:** HIGH

### Conclusion C2: Whether the gap is real or noise is currently indeterminate

GT-2 (no SD/raw data given) + GT-3 (small-sample CI/significance requires SD or raw data)
→ the inputs a reader would need to compute a confidence interval or run a significance test on the 62%-vs-71% comparison are exactly the inputs the report omits
→ whether the 9-point difference reflects a real effect of the catalyst or ordinary run-to-run variation cannot be determined from the report as given

**Pre-check:** head GT-2, GT-3 · ?-marked: none · lowest cited: none · Inputs ceiling: HIGH
**Confidence:** HIGH

### Conclusion C3: A 9-point gap at n=3 is well within reach of ordinary sampling noise

GT-3 (small-sample CI mechanics) + GT-4 (n=3 illustration, mean 56%, CI 30–82%) + GT-5 (n=7 illustration, mean 57%, CI 52–63%)
→ at n=3, a spread of individual values that is not itself extreme (45%, 56%, 66%) already produces a 95% confidence interval about 52 points wide, roughly ±26 points around the mean *[Assumes: A13]*
→ raising the replicate count to n=7 with comparable underlying scatter narrows that interval to about 11 points wide, without requiring any reduction in per-run variability
→ a 9-point difference between two n=3 means sits well inside the kind of uncertainty band ordinary small-sample scatter alone can produce, so the reported gap cannot currently be distinguished from noise, and the direct remedy is more replicates or a reported spread — not accepting or dismissing the 71% figure outright

**Pre-check:** head GT-3, GT-4, GT-5 · ?-marked: none · lowest cited: none · Inputs ceiling: HIGH
**Confidence:** LOW — two axes are short. Inference: A13 (the illustrative dataset's scatter stands in for plausible real reaction scatter) is unpriced — if this specific reaction's actual measurement precision is much tighter than the illustration (e.g., automated analytical quantitation), the endpoint would flip toward "the gap is likely real," so the endpoint does not survive A13 failing. Rivals: the competing reading — "this reaction's method is precise enough that 9 points is real" — is live and unsettled by anything in this analysis. What would close both: the lab's actual per-run yields (or SD) for both conditions.

### Conclusion C4: Causal attribution to "the catalyst" specifically is not established

GT-2 (no stated controls) + GT-6 (causal attribution requires a controlled comparison)
→ the report supplies no evidence ruling out other differences between the two sets of runs — conditions, measurement method, or run selection — as the source of the observed gap
→ attributing the increase specifically to "the catalyst," as opposed to some other uncontrolled difference between the two sets of runs, is not established by the report as given

**Pre-check:** head GT-2, GT-6 · ?-marked: none · lowest cited: none · Inputs ceiling: HIGH
**Confidence:** MEDIUM — Rivals axis short: the live rival "conditions actually were held constant but simply weren't mentioned in the shorthand report" is not ruled out anywhere in this analysis. What would close it: the lab's methods section or SI describing both conditions.

### Conclusion C5: The practical stakes compound the longer the number goes unverified

C1 (observed comparison established) + C2 (real-vs-noise indeterminate) + GT-7 (regression toward the mean)
→[2nd] a reader who treats the reported 71% as already validated may commit resources — scale-up planning, further formulation work, citing the figure downstream — before the effect is confirmed by replication *[Assumes: A14]*
→[3rd] if the reported figure is in part a favorable draw from a noisy 3-run sample, replication would on average pull the observed effect back toward the true value, and by the time that correction surfaces the 71% figure may already be cited elsewhere as settled *[Assumes: A15]*
→ the practical stakes of the report scale with how it is used downstream, so the appropriate response is to seek replication and variance data before treating 71% as a reliable planning figure, rather than either accepting or dismissing the claim outright

**Pre-check:** head C1 (HIGH), C2 (HIGH), GT-7 · ?-marked: none · lowest cited: HIGH · Inputs ceiling: HIGH
**Confidence:** LOW — Inference axis short: A14 is unpriced (if no one actually acts on n=3, no-variance data without further evidence, the downstream-risk hop does not hold, and the endpoint does not survive A14 failing). Rivals axis short: the competing view "no reasonable actor commits real resources on this thin a report, so the downstream risk is negligible" is live and unsettled. What would close it: evidence of how this specific report is actually being used.

### Conclusion C6: A confirmed effect here would still not establish generalizability or value

C1 (observed comparison established) + GT-2 (report omits substrate scope, cost, selectivity, scale)
→ the report's informational scope is limited to a single yield figure for what appears to be one reaction system, with no substrate-scope, cost, selectivity, or scale data given
→ even a fully confirmed, causally-attributed 62%→71% improvement under these exact conditions would not by itself establish that the catalyst is broadly useful, economically favorable, or practical to scale — those are separate questions the report does not address

**Pre-check:** head C1 (HIGH), GT-2 · ?-marked: none · lowest cited: HIGH · Inputs ceiling: HIGH
**Confidence:** HIGH

---

## 5. Abandoned Reasoning

**Dead End 1: Treating "typical" organic-synthesis replicate-yield variance as a directly citable empirical ground truth.**
What was tried: searched for and attempted to fetch a peer-reviewed source (a Thieme-published letter on reaction-yield uncertainty reporting) and its open preprint (the Zenodo primer) to obtain an empirical figure for typical run-to-run standard deviation in bench-scale organic yields.
Why abandoned: the Thieme source was unreachable (bot/JS-protection interstitial, not article content — see Phase 3 failure record). The Zenodo primer was reachable and read in full, but its numeric example is explicitly labeled "imagined" test data — a synthetic teaching illustration for computing a CI/plot — not measured replicate data, so it cannot support an empirical "typical variance" claim without overclaiming from source.
What it ruled out: using this material as an unqualified empirical ground truth for "typical chemistry yield noise," which would have let the analysis claim too strongly that the reported 9-point gap is *probably* noise. This is why the primer's numbers are used only as a mathematical illustration of CI-arithmetic sensitivity to n (GT-4/GT-5, chain C3), explicitly caveated, while A12 (the empirical magnitude claim) stays flagged unverified.

**Dead End 2: Applying a full categorical fishbone brainstorm to the assumption space.**
What was tried: considered mapping the claim's hidden assumptions onto a fixed category set (e.g., People/Process/Technology/Environment/Information/Resources) before building the Assumptions Table.
Why abandoned: the assumption space here is a single evidentiary/methodological claim with a small, directly enumerable set of dependencies (what was held constant, how "three runs" and "yield" are defined, whether reporting was selective, whether the effect generalizes), fully surfaced by direct inversion-style reasoning (Phase 2) without category scaffolding; forcing these into categories built for production/service/knowledge-work contexts would have produced several empty or artificial buckets rather than added coverage.
What it ruled out: a category-first assumption pass for this problem; direct inversion-based enumeration is what actually surfaced the load-bearing preconditions (A1, A4, A5, A6, A11) used in the chains.

---

## 6. Conclusion

**What can be concluded (directly from the report's own content):**
- The report establishes that a mean yield increase from 62% to 71% (9 percentage points absolute, ≈14.5% relative) was observed and reported by the lab, based on three runs (chain C1).
- The report, as stated, does not specify the run-to-run spread, the exact definition of "three runs," or whether conditions were held constant, so its literal content is limited to that single point-to-point comparison (chain C1).
- Even a fully confirmed and correctly-attributed effect at this scale would say nothing about the catalyst's value on other substrates, its cost, selectivity, or scalability, none of which the report addresses (chain C6).

**What cannot be concluded (and why):**
- That the 9-point difference is statistically distinguishable from ordinary run-to-run noise — no standard deviation, range, or raw values are given, and no significance test or confidence interval can be computed without them (chain C2).
- That the 9-point gap is even a plausible signal rather than noise — an illustrative n=3 dataset with an unremarkable spread already produces a 95% confidence interval roughly 52 points wide, so a 9-point difference between two 3-run means is easily within reach of ordinary scatter alone (chain C3).
- That the increase was caused specifically by the catalyst — the report gives no basis for ruling out other differences (conditions, measurement method, or run selection) between the two sets of runs (chain C4).
- That the 71% figure generalizes to other substrates or scales, or is economically favorable — the report addresses only yield for what appears to be a single reaction (chain C6).
- That the number is a reliable, already-settled planning figure — small, unreplicated samples are exactly the kind of result that regresses toward a smaller true effect on replication, so downstream decisions should wait for confirmation rather than treat 71% as fixed (chain C5).

# First-Principles Analysis: The 62%→71% Catalyst Yield Claim

*(MODE = full-composer; no single-technique trigger fired in the request, so all five phases run, with inversion, estimate, and second-order thinking applied where each phase invokes them.)*

## 1. Problem Essence

**Core problem:** Does the reported comparison (mean yield 62% → 71%, three runs) by itself provide sufficient evidence that a specific manipulated variable — the new catalyst — caused a real, statistically distinguishable, reproducible, generalizable improvement in this reaction's yield, and, if not, exactly which weaker claims does the data still support versus merely permit as speculation?

**Success criteria** (checkable against the Conclusion, section 6):
1. Section 6 lists, as specific claims, what is supported by the report's literal content alone — each such claim cites only the literal-content chains (C1, C6) and introduces no unstated assumption.
2. Section 6 lists, as specific claims, which stronger claims (statistical significance, real-effect-vs-noise, causal attribution to the catalyst, generalizability/economic value, reliability as a planning figure) are *not* supported, and each names the concrete missing datum (SD/raw values, controls statement, substrate scope, replicate count) that would resolve it.
3. At least one quantitative treatment (the estimate technique) shows, with an actual worked and independently-recomputed confidence-interval calculation, how wide the uncertainty band around an n=3 mean can be — this is a checkable property of the Ground Truths/Derivation Chains, not an assertion.
4. No chain in section 4 that section 6 relies on asserts, at HIGH confidence, either "the catalyst works" or "the catalyst doesn't work" — the Conclusion's confidence rating is calibrated to what the evidence actually licenses, not to a verdict either direction.

---

## 2. Assumptions Table

Phase 2 inversion was applied to the headline claim ("the catalyst raises yield from 62% to 71%"). Inverted form: "the catalyst does not raise yield; the 9-point gap is not attributable to it." Failure-guaranteeing conditions enumerated: (a) run-to-run process variability alone could produce a 9-point gap; (b) the baseline and catalyzed runs were not run under matched conditions; (c) the three reported runs were selected from a larger, partially unreported set; (d) yield was measured by different methods in the two conditions; (e) the runs are not independent (shared reagent lot, shared workup); (f) a 9-point gap is not chemically distinguishable from ordinary measurement noise for this class of reaction. Each necessary precondition of the original claim is recorded below as an `untested belief`, tagged load-bearing where the conclusion does not survive its failure.

| # | Assumption | Type | Treatment | Verdict | Verification |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A1 | The 62% baseline was obtained under the same conditions (temperature, stoichiometry, solvent, workup, timing, substrate batch) as the 71% catalyzed runs — a true controlled comparison. **[load-bearing]** | untested belief | Verify or flag | Challenge — the report gives no statement either way; this is inversion's single most load-bearing precondition | unverified — flagged |
| A2 | "Three runs" means three independent replicates of the catalyzed condition (and, separately, of the baseline) — not one batch measured three times, not a mixed count. | untested belief | Verify or flag | Challenge — the phrase is genuinely ambiguous as worded | unverified — flagged |
| A3 | 62% and 71% are arithmetic means of the three runs, not a best-of-three or a single rounded representative run. | untested belief | Verify or flag | Challenge — no statement of how the reported figure was derived from the three runs | unverified — flagged |
| A4 | Yield was measured by the same method (e.g., isolated yield after identical purification) in both conditions. **[load-bearing]** | untested belief | Verify or flag | Challenge — measurement-method mismatch is a known source of spurious "improvement" | unverified — flagged |
| A5 | The three reported runs are the complete set of attempts made — no lower-yielding or failed runs were excluded before reporting. **[load-bearing]** | untested belief | Verify or flag | Challenge — selective reporting is a well-documented risk pattern and cannot be excluded from the report alone | unverified — flagged |
| A6 | The runs are statistically independent (not correlated through a shared reagent batch, shared workup step, or same-day operator effects). **[load-bearing]** | untested belief | Verify or flag | Challenge — nothing in the report addresses this | unverified — flagged |
| A7 | Reporting a mean yield across three runs with no stated spread is an acceptable convention in this context. | convention | Challenge before accepting | Challenge — GT-3 shows current best-practice guidance explicitly argues this convention should be replaced by mean+95% CI reporting precisely because it hides this information | unverified — flagged |
| A8 | The underlying raw per-run data / supporting information (SI) is unavailable to this analysis. | current constraint | Record expiry | Accept — expires once the lab's SI, notebook, or raw data are obtained | current, as of this analysis |
| A9 | Yield alone is sufficient to judge whether "the catalyst" is valuable, without selectivity, loading/cost, turnover number, or recyclability data. | untested belief / convention | Challenge | Challenge — catalyst value is multidimensional; the report addresses only one dimension | unverified — flagged |
| A10 | The 9-point improvement generalizes beyond this one substrate/reaction/scale. | untested belief | Verify or flag | Challenge — no substrate-scope or scale-up data given | unverified — flagged |
| A11 | A 9-point (≈14.5% relative) yield difference is chemically meaningful rather than within ordinary run-to-run noise for this class of reaction. **[load-bearing]** | untested belief | Verify or flag | Challenge — this is exactly what cannot be judged without variance data (see GT-3, chains C2/C3) | unverified — flagged |
| A12 | Typical run-to-run standard deviation for manually executed bench-scale organic-yield measurements is on the order of several to ~10+ percentage points. | untested belief | Verify or flag | Challenge — attempted verification; the directly on-point source was unreachable and the open alternative uses synthetic, not measured, data (Phase 3 failure record below) | unverified — flagged, not promoted to a ground truth |
| A13 | The illustrative n=3/n=7 dataset used in chain C3 (synthetic "imagined" data from a methods primer) is a reasonable stand-in for the kind of scatter a real reaction's yield replicates could plausibly show. *(surfaced by End-of-phase Assumption Audit, chain C3 step 3)* | untested belief | Verify or flag | Challenge — the source itself labels this data "imagined"; used only as a mathematical illustration, not an empirical claim | unverified — flagged |
| A14 | At least some downstream readers/decision-makers would act on the 71% figure (scale-up planning, further citation) without first seeking replication or variance data. *(surfaced by Assumption Audit, chain C5 step 1)* | untested belief | Verify or flag | Challenge — plausible but not confirmed for this specific report | unverified — flagged |
| A15 | The reported 71% is a first/early small-sample result not already cross-checked against a larger confirmatory dataset — i.e., the kind of result regression-to-the-mean applies to. *(surfaced by Assumption Audit, chain C5 step 2)* | untested belief | Verify or flag | Challenge — consistent with "three runs" being described as if it were the whole evidentiary basis, but not confirmed | unverified — flagged |

---

## 3. Ground Truths

**GT-1** The report states that yield rose from 62% to 71%, "measured across three runs." — source: the problem statement supplied for this analysis; read-at-source: direct quotation, the claim text itself.

**GT-2** The report specifies no standard deviation, range, or confidence interval for either figure; does not state whether "three runs" refers to the catalyzed condition only, to both conditions, or to something else; and does not state whether reaction conditions (temperature, stoichiometry, catalyst loading, solvent, workup, timing, substrate batch) or the yield-measurement method were held constant between the two conditions. — source: same problem statement; read-at-source: verified by direct inspection — nothing beyond the quoted sentence is given.

**GT-3** For a small sample (n<30), the (1−α)100% confidence interval for a sample mean requires the sample standard deviation s_x (or the raw data points from which it is computed), in addition to n: x̄ ± t_(α/2)(s_x/√n), with (n−1) degrees of freedom; no CI or significance test can be computed without s_x or the raw values. — source: Sally Bloodworth, "Reporting uncertainty: an updated convention for organic chemists," Zenodo record 14999714 ("Primer.pdf"); read-at-source: p.7, Appendix "Confidence interval" formula, quoted directly.

**GT-4** In that primer's worked exemplar, three replicate yields for "Compound 3" (56%, 66%, 45%) give a mean of 56% and a stated 95% CI of 30%–82% — a 52-percentage-point-wide interval; the primer explicitly labels this "an imagined dataset" (synthetic/illustrative, not measured lab data). — source: same Zenodo Primer; read-at-source: p.2, Figure 1 (data table) and Figure 2 (Compound 3 panel); independently recomputed here (t₀.₀₂₅,₂ = 4.303, s_x ≈ 10.5, SE ≈ 6.07, 56 ± 26.1 ≈ 30–82) and matches the source exactly.

**GT-5** In the same exemplar, "Compound 1" with seven replicate yields (56, 66, 45, 58, 59, 60, 58) gives a mean of 57% and a stated 95% CI of 52%–63% — an 11-point-wide interval, markedly narrower than Compound 3's despite comparable individual-value scatter (45–66). — source: same Zenodo Primer; read-at-source: p.2, Figure 1/Figure 2, Compound 1; independently recomputed here (mean 57.4, s_x ≈ 6.32, SE ≈ 2.39, t₀.₀₂₅,₆=2.447, CI ≈ 51.6–63.3) and matches the source.

**GT-6** Attributing an observed difference in an outcome specifically to one manipulated variable (here, the catalyst) requires that other variables capable of affecting the outcome were held constant between the compared conditions; if other variables could also have differed, the observed difference is logically consistent with any of those variables, singly or in combination, and cannot be uniquely assigned to the variable of interest without further evidence. — source: derivation shown inline (definition of a controlled comparison; yield is known to depend on multiple factors — temperature, stoichiometry, workup, measurement method — so an uncontrolled comparison under-determines the cause); classified as a matter of formal/methodological logic, not an external citation.

**GT-7** Regression toward the mean: when a value is observed to be unusually extreme partly because of random (noise) variation, an independent later measurement of the same underlying quantity will, on average, be less extreme than the originally observed value, because the specific noise draw that produced the extremity is not expected to recur. — source: derivation shown inline via variance decomposition (observed = true effect + independent noise; conditioning on an unusually high observed value raises the expected noise contribution, which does not repeat identically on remeasurement); the phenomenon is the standard one first described by Galton (1886) — no external citation opened for that historical attribution.

**Phase 3 failure record:** The source `https://www.thieme-connect.com/products/ejournals/pdf/10.1055/a-2907-9424.pdf` ("Letter: Standard Reporting of the Uncertainty in Reaction Yield," Thieme) — sought to verify A12 (typical real-world run-to-run yield variance) — could not be opened; WebFetch returned a bot-protection/"enable JavaScript and cookies" interstitial rather than article content. Reason: unreachable. The open alternative located (the Zenodo primer above, by the same author/topic) was read in full and satisfies GT-3/GT-4/GT-5, but it uses explicitly synthetic ("imagined") illustrative data, so it does **not** verify A12's empirical magnitude claim; A12 remains unverified and was deliberately not promoted to a ground truth (see Abandoned Reasoning, Dead End 1).

**Provenance summary:** `?`-marked: none (0 of 7). Read-at-source: GT-1 (problem statement, direct quote), GT-2 (problem statement, absence verified by inspection), GT-3 (Primer p.7), GT-4 (Primer p.2), GT-5 (Primer p.2). GT-6 and GT-7 are verified by inline derivation rather than external citation; neither feeds a HIGH-confidence chain on its own (GT-6 → C4, MEDIUM; GT-7 → C5, LOW), so Criterion 3's read-at-source-location requirement for HIGH chains does not apply to them.

---

## 4. Derivation Chains

### Conclusion C1: The report's literal content is limited to a bare point-to-point comparison

GT-1 (report's stated numbers: 62%→71%, three runs) + GT-2 (report omits SD, controls, run-definition)
→ the only information content the report carries is a comparison of two point-value averages, obtained under conditions the report does not specify
→ taken at face value, the report licenses stating only that a mean-yield increase was observed and reported — nothing beyond that

**Pre-check:** head GT-1, GT-2 · ?-marked: none · lowest cited: none · Inputs ceiling: HIGH
**Confidence:** HIGH

### Conclusion C2: Whether the gap is real or noise is currently indeterminate

GT-2 (no SD/raw data given) + GT-3 (small-sample CI/significance requires SD or raw data)
→ the inputs a reader would need to compute a confidence interval or run a significance test on the 62%-vs-71% comparison are exactly the inputs the report omits
→ whether the 9-point difference reflects a real effect of the catalyst or ordinary run-to-run variation cannot be determined from the report as given

**Pre-check:** head GT-2, GT-3 · ?-marked: none · lowest cited: none · Inputs ceiling: HIGH
**Confidence:** HIGH

### Conclusion C3: A 9-point gap at n=3 is well within reach of ordinary sampling noise

GT-3 (small-sample CI mechanics) + GT-4 (n=3 illustration, mean 56%, CI 30–82%) + GT-5 (n=7 illustration, mean 57%, CI 52–63%)
→ at n=3, a spread of individual values that is not itself extreme (45%, 56%, 66%) already produces a 95% confidence interval about 52 points wide, roughly ±26 points around the mean *[Assumes: A13]*

- A mean yield increase from 62% to 71% (9 points absolute, ~14.5% relative) was observed and reported, based on three runs.
- That's it, at face value — the report is a bare point-to-point comparison. **That the gap is real rather than noise.** No standard deviation, range, or raw values are given, so no confidence interval or significance test can be computed — the report is missing the exact inputs needed to answer this. Bumping to n=7 with similar scatter narrows the interval to roughly ±5–6 points — replicate count matters more than most people intuit here.

**That the catalyst caused it.** Attributing the change to "the catalyst" specifically requires that everything else was held constant. The report doesn't say this. Any other uncontrolled difference (reagent batch, operator, day, measurement method) is an equally live explanation.

**That it generalizes or matters practically.** One reaction, presumably one substrate, no cost/selectivity/loading/scalability data. Even a fully confirmed 9-point gain here says nothing about whether the catalyst is useful broadly.

**That 71% is a stable number worth planning around.** A promising early result from a small, unreplicated sample is exactly the kind of figure that tends to shrink toward the true effect on replication (regression to the mean). Treating it as settled before confirming risks anchoring downstream decisions to a number that won't hold up.

## Bottom line
The honest read is "preliminary, promising, unconfirmed" — not "the catalyst works" and not "the catalyst doesn't work." The concrete fix is cheap: get the per-run values (or at least the SD) for both conditions, confirm conditions were matched, and run more replicates. The arithmetic of small samples, not any suspicion about the chemistry, is what makes the current claim indeterminate.
